subtype: Approach: following up with a thank-you and progress [Revision]
passage: My name is Noor, and for two years I only went to my professor when I was drowning. I would ask, get an answer, mumble thanks and vanish. Then the professor said at the end of one meeting, "Let me know how it goes." I noticed that I never had. So this time I fixed the errors and the next day sent a short message: "Thank you for Tuesday. Your tip about the boundary condition fixed the whole second section." Two weeks later I brought a new draft and a fresh question. The professor remembered the earlier one. I had always thought asking for help was a single favour. It turned out to be the start of a conversation.

qa.q: What did Noor's professor say at the end of the meeting?
qa.a: The professor said, Let me know how it goes.

qa.q: What did Noor realise after the professor's remark?
qa.a: Noor felt a little embarrassed on noticing that Noor had never reported back after getting help, and understood that a thank-you with progress was missing.

qa.q: What else could Noor do to keep the relationship going, and why?
qa.a: Noor could share a short note whenever a paper or project reaches a milestone, because small updates show the professor's time had an effect.

qa.q: How might the professor see students who return with progress?
qa.a: The professor likely feels the time was well spent and is more willing to help again, since the students show what the advice achieved.

grounding: After a meeting a student sends thanks with what was fixed and later returns with new work, turning a favour into an ongoing relationship.
